balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Lam Research Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Lam Research Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Lam Research Corporation: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Lam Research Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Lam Research Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Lam Research Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Lam Research Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Lam Research Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

regionRevenue.title: Revenue by customer region
regionRevenue.content:
Semiconductor capital equipment revenue booked by the customer's region -- where the fab sits, not where Lam's own operations are.

For Lam Research: China was ~30-37% of revenue in FY2022-23 as domestic fabs rushed to buy equipment ahead of expanding US export controls, then spiked further as China stockpiled before rules tightened. Korea, Taiwan, Japan and the US track the capex cycles of Samsung/SK Hynix, TSMC, the Japanese memory/foundry players and Intel/Micron respectively.

What to watch:

  • China share falling as export-control carve-outs narrow which tools can still ship there
  • Korea/Taiwan swings tracking memory and leading-edge foundry capex cycles, not Lam-specific demand
  • Any region's revenue is as much a license/entity-list decision as a demand signal

chinaExposure.title: China and customer concentration
chinaExposure.content:
China's share of revenue, and the largest single customer's share, both derived against total revenue each period.

For Lam Research: China ran above 40% of revenue in FY2024 as domestic customers front-loaded purchases of tools not yet restricted; it stepped back down to roughly a third of revenue by FY2026 as the restricted-tool list widened and that one-off pull-forward rolled off. A single customer has been in the mid-teens of revenue in recent years -- plausibly a large foundry or memory customer whose own capex plans move a meaningful slice of Lam's top line.

What to watch:

  • Further step-downs in China % following new export-control rounds (new restrictions announced after a quarter closes often show up a quarter or two later as backlog unwinds)
  • Largest-customer % rising, which raises customer-concentration risk even as geographic diversification improves

systemsService.title: Systems vs. customer support revenue
systemsService.content:
Systems revenue is new equipment shipped into fabs -- cyclical, tied to customers' capex budgets. Customer support (service) revenue covers spares, upgrades and the installed base's ongoing usage -- stickier and less cyclical because it scales with the installed tool base rather than this year's capex.

For Lam Research: service revenue held up far better than systems revenue in the FY2024 systems downturn, cushioning the overall decline -- the mix shift toward service in a weak year is itself a signal of the installed base's size and age.

What to watch:

  • Service revenue growing steadily through the cycle while systems revenue swings with capex spending
  • Systems revenue reaccelerating ahead of a reported fab capex upturn (orders lead revenue)

rd.title: R&D spend and intensity
rd.content:
R&D expense is cash and non-cash spend on new tool development; R&D intensity is that spend as a percentage of revenue.

For Lam Research: R&D has grown every year shown even through the FY2024 revenue downturn, because next-generation etch and deposition tools for GAA transistors and advanced packaging are multi-year programs that can't be throttled with the capex cycle -- intensity rises when revenue dips and falls back when revenue recovers.

What to watch:

  • R&D intensity spiking in a downturn (fixed program spend against a smaller revenue base) rather than cyclically cut
  • R&D growth rate versus the semiconductor equipment TAM's growth rate

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Lam Research Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Lam Research Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
